unit.title: Your team's story
unit.summary: Personalised: your team's identity, history, car and drivers, and how their fans talk.

lessons.title: {{team}}: who they are
lessons.objective: Say what {{team}} is known for, in one honest sentence.

payload.prompt: What does it mean that {{team}} is a constructor?

options.text: It enters its own cars in the championship and scores points in the constructors' standings.
options.explanation: Right. Every team on the grid is a constructor, and their points are added together for the team title.

options.text: It builds every single part of its car and engine itself.
options.explanation: Not necessarily. Many teams buy their power unit, and some buy other parts too.

options.text: It owns the circuit where its home race is held.
options.explanation: Owning a circuit has nothing to do with being a constructor.

options.text: It is only a constructor if it has won the title.
options.explanation: Every team entered in the championship is a constructor, whether it has won or not.

explanation.correct: A constructor is a team that enters its own cars in the championship. Both drivers' points add together for the constructors' title.
explanation.incorrect: Being a constructor is about entering the championship as a team and scoring constructors' points, not about building every part.
explanation.sayThisLine: Every team on the grid is a constructor.

payload.prompt: Which clue shows {{team}} is a customer team, not a works team?

options.text: Its power unit is built by a different company.
options.explanation: Right. Buying the power unit from a supplier is what makes a team a customer.

options.text: Its cars are painted in a different colour from last year.
options.explanation: Colours change for sponsors and style. They say nothing about who builds the power unit.

options.text: Its drivers are new to the team.
options.explanation: Driver changes do not change whether a team builds its own power unit.

options.text: It has not won a race recently.
options.explanation: Race results do not decide works or customer status. Both kinds of team win.

explanation.correct: A works team builds its own power unit. A customer team buys one from a supplier. The clue is always who built the power unit.
explanation.incorrect: Works or customer is about who builds the power unit, not results, colours or drivers.

payload.prompt: Can a customer team still win races and titles?

scene.alt: Text only: can a team that buys its power unit win?

explanation.correct: A good chassis on a good power unit can win. A customer team, McLaren on Mercedes power, won the 2025 constructors' title.
explanation.incorrect: Customer teams win too. What matters is how good the whole car is, not who built the power unit.
explanation.sayThisLine: Customer teams win too, so ask how good the whole car is.

statement.speaker: Someone at a watch party
statement.text: So who is {{team}} to you? Give me one honest sentence.

payload.question: What is the best honest answer?

options.text: I know their colours and their drivers, but tell me what you love about them.
options.explanation: Right. You say what you know and invite her story. It is honest and warm.

options.text: {{team}} is obviously the best team in the world and always will be.
options.explanation: That is blind fandom, and it shuts down the conversation.

options.text: I read all about their budget and wind-tunnel hours last night.
options.explanation: Do not fake expertise. You can sound knowledgeable by asking, not reciting.

options.text: I do not know anything about them and I do not care.
options.explanation: Honesty is great, but this one tells her you are not interested.

payload.translation: Say what you actually know, like colours and drivers, and invite her to tell you why she loves {{team}}.

followUps.line: What made you a {{team}} fan?
followUps.why: Fandom usually starts with a story. Asking for it is the best opener.

followUps.line: What is your favourite {{team}} moment?
followUps.why: It invites joy and gives you something real to remember.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know their whole history. Being curious is the point.

lessons.title: {{team}}: eras and rivalries
lessons.objective: Place {{team}}'s peaks and slumps and who they fight.

payload.prompt: Why is 2026 a fresh start for {{team}} and everyone else?

options.text: New rules reset the pecking order, so earlier form says less about who is quick now.
options.explanation: Right. A new regulation era means every team designs a new kind of car.

options.text: Every team starts the season with zero points and equal cars.
options.explanation: Points reset every year, but the cars are not equal. Teams have different designs.

options.text: The FIA gives each team a car built to the same design.
options.explanation: Teams design their own cars inside the rules.

options.text: The same teams always win, so nothing is fresh.
options.explanation: Not true. New eras often reshuffle the order.

explanation.correct: A new regulation era means new cars, so past form is a weaker guide. Teams that read the rules best can jump up or fall back.
explanation.incorrect: New rules mean new cars. The order can change a lot, which is why 2026 is exciting.

payload.prompt: What is a regulation era in Formula 1?

options.text: A season where one team wins a lot of races.
options.explanation: That is a winning season. An era is longer and is about the rules.

options.text: A multi-year rulebook cycle, after which the rules change and the order can reset.
options.explanation: Right. 2026 began a new one.

options.text: The years one driver wins many titles.
options.explanation: That is a driver's peak. A regulation era is about the cars and rules.

options.text: Any period when a team dominates.
options.explanation: Dominance can happen in an era, but the era itself is the rulebook.

explanation.correct: A regulation era is a cycle of car rules. When it changes, teams build new kinds of car and the pecking order can reshuffle.
explanation.incorrect: An era is defined by the rulebook, not by who is winning. When the rules change, a new era begins.
explanation.sayThisLine: A new era means a new rulebook.

options.text: Whichever teams are close enough to fight them for points and podiums, which can change.
options.explanation: Right. On track, rivals are whoever is near them that season.

options.text: The same team every single year.
options.explanation: Rivalries shift when the pecking order shifts.

options.text: Any team with a different colour car.
options.explanation: Colour has nothing to do with rivalry.

options.text: Whoever has the most money.
options.explanation: Money helps, but a rival is about results on track.

explanation.correct: On track, rivals are the teams fighting for the same positions. Fans also have historic rivalries, which do not always match the current order.
explanation.incorrect: A team's main rival is whoever it is fighting most closely that season. That can change.
explanation.sayThisLine: Who are they fighting with this year?

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: Every team has good years and bad years. Mine is just waiting for the next good one.

payload.question: What do you say?

options.text: Which year do you remember as the best one?
options.explanation: Right. You invite her to share her favourite memory, which is what she wants to talk about.

options.text: Sounds like they are finished.
options.explanation: That is unkind, and F1 resets often enough to keep hope alive.

options.text: That is just how it goes, and nobody can change it.
options.explanation: It is a dull reply and ignores the chance that new rules could change things.

options.text: So the drivers must have got worse?
options.explanation: Blaming the drivers skips the usual causes, like new rules, key staff changes and car development.

payload.translation: Every team has peaks and slumps, often tied to new rules or key people. Asking about her best memory is warm and honest.

followUps.line: Do the new rules give {{team}} a chance to come back?
followUps.why: A new regulation era can reset the pecking order, so it is a fair hopeful question.

followUps.line: Who were the stars of that golden era?
followUps.why: It shows you are interested in the people, not just the results.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to know the team's history. Asking is better than guessing.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: Will {{team}} win the championship this year? What do you think?

payload.question: What is the honest answer?

options.text: I am still learning, but it depends on how fast they develop the car and how reliable it is.
options.explanation: Right. You named the real factors without pretending to know.

options.text: Of course. Nobody can stop them.
options.explanation: That is blind optimism. Titles are never certain.

options.text: No chance. They are hopeless.
options.explanation: That is unkind, and you do not know enough to say it.

options.text: Ask me after I have looked at the standings.
options.explanation: Fine to check the standings, but it reads as a brush-off. Give her something real.

payload.translation: Championship chances depend on car development, reliability, luck and what the other teams do.

followUps.line: Do you think the car or the power unit is their biggest strength right now?
followUps.why: It shows you know there are two parts to performance.

followUps.line: Which team worries you most?
followUps.why: It lets her share what she is watching.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Saying you are still learning is fine. Name what you understand and ask her view.

payload.prompt: Put a regulation era in order.

items.text: The FIA announces new car rules
Teams design and build new cars
items.why: Each team interprets the rules in its own way.
Teams that read the rules best can jump up; others fall back.
Teams keep bringing upgrades to catch up or pull clear.
Eras last a few years before the rulebook changes again.

explanation.correct: New rules, new cars, a reset pecking order, a development race, and then the next rule change. That is why new eras are so exciting.
explanation.incorrect: The cycle is rules first, then new cars, then a reset order, then a development race, and eventually the next rule change.
explanation.sayThisLine: New rules mean the order gets shuffled.

lessons.title: {{team}}'s car and power unit now
lessons.objective: Explain {{team}}'s 2026 power unit and what it means.

payload.prompt: What is the 2026 power unit made of?

options.text: A V10 engine plus a battery.
options.explanation: F1 stopped using V10 engines long ago. It is a V6.

options.text: A turbo V6 engine plus an electric motor-generator, sharing the work roughly half and half.
options.explanation: Right. The engine and the electrical system are close to equal partners.

options.text: A fully electric motor with no engine.
options.explanation: That would be Formula E. F1 still has a combustion engine.

options.text: Two turbo engines side by side.
options.explanation: Each car has one engine and one electrical system.

explanation.correct: The 2026 power unit is a 1.6 litre turbo V6 plus an MGU-K electric motor-generator. The MGU-H was removed, and power is split roughly half and half.
explanation.incorrect: It is a turbo V6 plus an electric motor-generator, with the electrical side much bigger than before.
explanation.sayThisLine: 2026 power units are about half electric.

payload.prompt: Two teams share a power unit supplier. Will they be equally fast?

scene.alt: Text only: two teams using the same supplier's power unit.

explanation.correct: The power unit is only part of the car. Chassis, aero, strategy and drivers can make two teams on the same engine very different in pace.
explanation.incorrect: Sharing a supplier does not make teams equal. The rest of the car and the team matter a lot.

payload.prompt: Why does the power unit matter so much for {{team}}?

options.text: It supplies about half the car's power, so it shapes speed and reliability.
options.explanation: Right. A strong power unit helps everywhere, and a weak one costs time on every straight.

options.text: It decides how the car looks.
options.explanation: Looks come from the chassis and bodywork, not the power unit.

options.text: It only matters in qualifying.
options.explanation: It matters in qualifying and in the race.

options.text: It does not matter because the chassis is everything.
options.explanation: Both matter, and the 2026 rules make the power unit even more important.

explanation.correct: About half of the car's power comes from the electrical side and half from the engine, so the power unit shapes speed, energy management and reliability.
explanation.incorrect: The power unit is a huge part of performance. In 2026 it is also a huge part of race strategy, because energy management matters.
explanation.sayThisLine: The power unit is half the story.

payload.prompt: Match each term to what it means.

pairs.definition: The turbo V6 engine plus the electrical system, together.
Extra upgrade chances for power unit makers who fall well behind.
A company that builds power units and provides them to teams.
A team that races with a power unit built by another company.

distractorDefinitions: A test of how much fuel a car burns per lap.
A championship bonus for the most improved team.

explanation.summary: The power unit is the engine and electrical system together. Suppliers build them, customer teams buy them, and ADUO gives a safety net to makers who are behind.

lessons.title: {{driver}} and {{team}}'s line-up
lessons.objective: Know your person's driver, their teammate and the story between them.

payload.prompt: How do you fairly judge {{driver}} against their teammate?

options.text: Compare qualifying and race results across many weekends, not just one.
options.explanation: Right. A pattern across a season tells you much more than a single result.

options.text: Only look at who won the most recent race.
options.explanation: One race can be luck, strategy or an incident.

options.text: Compare them to drivers in other teams instead.
options.explanation: Other teams have different cars, so that is a weaker comparison.

options.text: Ask which driver is more famous.
options.explanation: Fame has nothing to do with pace.

explanation.correct: Teammates share a car, so looking at qualifying and race results across many weekends gives a fair read of who is quicker and when.
explanation.incorrect: A fair comparison uses a pattern, not a single result. Look at qualifying and races across a season.
explanation.sayThisLine: Over a season, how do they compare?

payload.prompt: {{driver}} is out-qualified by their teammate. What does that tell you?

options.text: The teammate was quicker over one lap that day. It is not the whole story.
options.explanation: Right. Qualifying is one lap. Race pace may tell a different tale.

options.text: {{driver}} is slower at everything.
options.explanation: One lap and a race are different skills.

options.text: {{driver}} will never beat their teammate.
options.explanation: One result cannot say that.

options.text: {{driver}} did not try.
options.explanation: Everyone pushes in qualifying. A gap is usually about pace or small mistakes.

explanation.correct: Qualifying measures one-lap pace. A gap on Saturday says something, but race pace and consistency matter too.
explanation.incorrect: A qualifying gap is one data point. Look at race pace as well.
explanation.sayThisLine: Qualifying is one lap; the race is a long story.

payload.template: A team order is an {{what}} from the team telling one driver to {{do}} for the benefit of the {{who}}.

explanation.correct: A team order is an instruction, like letting a teammate through or holding position. It puts the team's goals, such as the constructors' title, ahead of one driver.
explanation.incorrect: Team orders are instructions from the team to a driver, usually to let a teammate pass or hold station.
explanation.sayThisLine: They asked him to let his teammate through.

statement.speaker: A {{driver}} fan
statement.text: Is {{driver}} good? What do you think of them?

payload.question: What is the best honest reply?

options.text: I have only seen a bit, but what I liked was... What do you rate most about them?
options.explanation: Right. You share something real, then ask. That is honest and warm.

options.text: They are the greatest driver of all time.
options.explanation: That is overblown and not true to what you know.

options.text: Not really. There are much better drivers out there.
options.explanation: It is a blunt dismissal of her favourite driver.

options.text: Their stats are brilliant, and I have memorised all of them.
options.explanation: Do not fake expertise. A single honest detail is better than an invented pile of stats.

payload.translation: Share one real thing you have noticed about {{driver}}, then ask what she rates most.

followUps.line: What was the best race you saw them drive?
followUps.why: It invites her to relive a favourite moment.

followUps.line: How do they compare with their teammate?
followUps.why: A teammate is the fairest benchmark in F1.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: One honest observation is worth more than a pile of stats.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: Sometimes {{driver}} gets beaten by their teammate and it stings.

payload.question: What do you say?

options.text: That sounds tough. Do you think it is pace, or just a bad weekend?
options.explanation: Right. You acknowledge her feeling and ask her to reason about it.

options.text: That proves the teammate is simply better.
options.explanation: One result proves nothing. It is also not kind to a fan.

options.text: Everyone gets beaten sometimes. Get over it.
options.explanation: That is dismissive of how she feels.

options.text: The team probably gives them the better car.
options.explanation: Teammates have the same car, so this is unlikely and unfair to the team.

payload.translation: Being beaten by a teammate hurts because it is the fairest comparison. Asking whether it is pace or just a bad weekend shows you care.

followUps.line: Do you think they can close the gap?
followUps.why: It turns frustration into hopeful analysis.

followUps.line: What has helped them in the past?
followUps.why: It invites her to share what she has seen.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to fix it. Listening is the point.

lessons.title: How {{team}} fans talk
lessons.objective: Recognise fan in-jokes and pet peeves without faking it.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: I am a {{team}} fan through and through. What do you think of us fans?

payload.question: What is the best reply?

options.text: You clearly care a lot. How did you get into {{team}}?
options.explanation: Right. You compliment without stereotyping and ask for her story.

options.text: {{team}} fans are all a bit mad.
options.explanation: A stereotype, even if meant kindly, does not respect what fandom means to her.

options.text: I do not really get why people support one team.
options.explanation: Honest but cold. Try curiosity instead.

options.text: Every {{team}} fan has the same opinions.
options.explanation: Fans disagree all the time. That is half the fun.

payload.translation: Fandom is personal. Asking how she got into {{team}} respects her loyalty.

followUps.line: What is your favourite {{team}} moment?
followUps.why: It invites joy rather than complaints.

followUps.line: How long have you followed them?
followUps.why: It gives you a sense of how much history she carries.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need to be a {{team}} fan yourself. Be respectful and curious.

payload.question: What do you whisper to the person next to you?

options.text: They just told {{driver}} to pit this lap for a set of mediums.
options.explanation: Right. You decoded it correctly: a pit call with the tyre choice.

options.text: {{driver}} is in trouble and has to stop.
options.explanation: Box box is a routine pit call, not a problem.

options.text: They want {{driver}} to slow down for a few laps.
options.explanation: That is a pace instruction, not a pit call.

options.text: It means a penalty.
options.explanation: A penalty would be announced differently.

payload.translation: Box box is the call to come into the pits, and the tyre name tells the driver what he is getting.

followUps.line: Why mediums?
followUps.why: The team chose the compound for how many laps remain and how worn the tyres are.

followUps.line: Is that an undercut?
followUps.why: It could be, if a rival just pitted and this stop is to beat them.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Radio shorthand is a language. Learning it is part of joining in.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: There are rumours about {{driver}} and next year's seat. Silly season is starting.

payload.question: How should you treat it?

options.text: As silly season talk: fun to discuss, but rumours until the team confirms it.
options.explanation: Right. The driver market is full of guesses, and few are true.

options.text: As a fact, since someone said it online.
options.explanation: Rumours are often wrong. Wait for a team announcement.

options.text: As nothing important.
options.explanation: The driver market matters to fans, so treat it with interest.

options.text: As proof that {{driver}} is unhappy.
options.explanation: Rumours say little about how a driver feels.

payload.translation: Silly season is the rumour period about driver moves. Treat stories as guesses until a team confirms them.

followUps.line: Where did you hear it?
followUps.why: A good question. The source tells you how seriously to take it.

followUps.line: Would you want them to stay?
followUps.why: It lets her share what she hopes.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: It is fine to say you only know it as a rumour. Asking her view is enough.

payload.title: {{team}} fan lingo
payload.setting: She is fuming about a {{team}} pit call after the race.

exchanges.theirMessage: That strategy call was awful. They boxed way too late.

replies.text: So they missed the window? What would have helped?
replies.theirResponse: Earlier, before the traffic. They left him out too long.
replies.coachNote: You asked what went wrong. That shows you are following the strategy.
True, but it does not invite her to explain. Ask what went wrong.

replies.text: Pit stops only take two seconds anyway.
replies.theirResponse: That is not the point. Timing matters.
replies.coachNote: The stop is quick, but the timing of the stop is everything.

payload.closingNote: Fans talk strategy in detail. Listen for their frustration with pit calls and timing.

lessons.title: Good questions to ask a {{team}} fan
lessons.objective: Ask three follow-ups that show you have been listening.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: I am so upset about today's race. The strategy was terrible and we lost.

payload.question: What do you ask?

options.text: Do you think it was the strategy, or did someone just have a faster car today?
options.explanation: Right. You help her separate strategy from car pace.

options.text: Yeah, the strategy was obviously wrong.
options.explanation: Piling on does not show you have thought about it. Ask her reasons.

options.text: So the strategists should be sacked?
options.explanation: That jumps to blame. Ask what she saw before deciding who was at fault.

options.text: It is only a sport. Calm down.
options.explanation: That dismisses what she feels.

payload.translation: Good questions turn a complaint into a conversation. Ask her to explain what she saw.

followUps.line: When would you have stopped?
followUps.why: It invites her to describe the call she wanted.

followUps.line: Does it change the season for them?
followUps.why: It keeps perspective beyond one race.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: You do not need an answer to her question. Asking is the skill.

statement.speaker: A {{team}} fan
statement.text: I am really optimistic about next season. I think {{team}} can be strong.

payload.question: What do you ask?

options.text: What makes you so optimistic? Is it the drivers, the car, or the rule changes?
options.explanation: Right. You ask for her reasons, and you give her three handy doors.

options.text: Sure, whatever.
options.explanation: Empty agreement shows you were not listening.

options.text: Optimism never works in F1.
options.explanation: That is a downer, and untrue. Plenty of teams bounce back.

options.text: I am sure they will win everything.
options.explanation: Do not promise results you cannot know.

payload.translation: Ask what is behind her hope. It shows you care and lets her do the talking.

followUps.line: What do you think they need most?
followUps.why: It helps her think through the team's challenges.

followUps.line: Who is the main threat?
followUps.why: It keeps the chat on the real competitive picture.

payload.noFakeExpertNote: Fans love to explain why they are hopeful. Let her.

payload.title: Talking about {{team}} change
payload.setting: She is worried about a change at {{team}}.

exchanges.theirMessage: {{team}} just changed their race engineer. I am nervous about it.

replies.text: What was the old engineer like? Why do you trust them more?
replies.theirResponse: He knew the car inside out. This new person has a lot to learn.
replies.coachNote: You asked her to explain her concern. That is respect.
You agreed, but you did not go deeper. Ask why she is worried.

replies.text: New people bring fresh ideas. It will be better.
replies.theirResponse: You do not know that. You do not follow {{team}}.
replies.coachNote: Dismissing her worry backfires. Listen first, then offer perspective.

exchanges.theirMessage: But maybe {{team}} needed a change. The car development has felt slow.

replies.text: So the old setup was holding them back?
replies.theirResponse: Maybe. Or maybe the team did not give him what he needed.
replies.coachNote: You let her work through it. That is the real skill.
Agree, but keep asking. She is thinking it through.

replies.text: Yeah, they have been bad for years.
replies.coachNote: Piling on does not help. Stick to what you know.

payload.closingNote: Team changes bring strong feelings. Listen to her history with the team before sharing your view.

payload.title: Finding common ground
payload.setting: A {{team}} fan is passionate and a little heartbroken.

exchanges.theirMessage: I love {{team}}, but they break my heart sometimes.

replies.text: That is the price of caring, right? What moment hurt the most?
replies.theirResponse: Oh, so many. But I am still here.
replies.coachNote: You validated her feeling and asked for her story. Perfect.
You do not have to have lived her heartbreak. Ask her to explain it.

replies.text: Why not just pick a winning team?
replies.theirResponse: That is not how it works.
replies.coachNote: Fandom is not rational. Respect that, even if it seems strange to you.

payload.closingNote: Loyalty is earned and tested. Listen to why she stays despite the pain.
